plot_extraction.response_text:
Colonel Aquila Telfair, a proud guardian of Southern tradition, becomes editor of a Georgia magazine devoted exclusively to Southern writers. He fills its pages with antiquated literature and contributions chosen more for their authors’ Confederate pedigrees and family connections than for merit, leaving the publication obscure and unprofitable.

T. T. Thacker, a practical New York magazine promoter, offers to invest in the magazine and expand its circulation by publishing popular work from prominent writers across the country. Though Telfair resists Northern influence, he reveals that he is considering an exceptional eight-thousand-word submission by a famous Northerner. He admires the article but refuses to print it until he can establish that its author has acceptable Southern connections.

Two weeks later, Thacker discovers that Telfair has published President Theodore Roosevelt’s message to Congress, presenting Roosevelt as a member of Georgia’s well-known Bulloch family through his maternal ancestry. Thus, Telfair admits Northern material only after finding a way to claim its author for the South.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story uses a brisk, urbane comic-satirical style, shaped by an amused third-person narrator who moves freely between straightforward exposition, caricature, and conversational asides. The narrative voice is confident and companionable, occasionally addressing the reader directly—“If you were familiar…” or “Well, sir, if you believe me”—and thereby creating the atmosphere of an anecdote told aloud. Although the narrator generally maintains an outwardly neutral manner, the selection and phrasing of details continually expose the absurdities of the characters and their institutions.

Its dominant tone is dryly ironic rather than openly condemnatory. The magazine’s devotion to Southern heritage is treated through affectionate but sustained ridicule: professional qualifications are replaced by Confederate ancestry, social connections, and increasingly remote encounters with famous historical figures. Comic escalation is central to this effect. The staff begins with plausible family associations and proceeds to such absurd credentials as an aunt once kissed by Stonewall Jackson and a child soldier carrying “a sword in one hand and a milk-bottle in the other.” Hyperbole, mock solemnity, bathos, and incongruous comparisons repeatedly puncture claims to dignity. Phrases such as “a whole crate of Georgia peaches” and “Even Georgia stock companies sometimes realize that it takes live ones to bury the dead” give the narration a punchy, aphoristic quality.

The diction is built around a sharp contrast between two verbal registers. Colonel Telfair speaks in ceremonious, Latinate, nineteenth-century prose, using balanced clauses, abstract nouns, formal courtesies, and circumlocutions. His language reflects erudition, pride, and social rigidity: he “desires to conform,” “institutes an investigation,” and objects to “jibes and derogatory comments.” Thacker, by contrast, speaks in compressed, energetic American business slang. His idiom is full of commercial terminology, topical references, jokes, wagers, and mixed metaphors: manuscripts are “truck,” weak material is “slush,” and a successful article must “make ’em sit up.” Their dialogue is therefore not merely functional but dramatic; each man’s vocabulary embodies a competing worldview—ancestral prestige and sectional loyalty on one side, circulation, novelty, and market value on the other.

Sentences in the narrative vary between expansive descriptive periods and short comic punches. Longer sentences accumulate names, credentials, historical references, and qualifications until the sheer excess becomes humorous. Short declarative sentences then deliver reversals or punch lines: “It was a whole crate of Georgia peaches.” Lists are especially important. They mimic the magazine’s overcrowded, indiscriminate contents while allowing the comedy to build item by item. Parenthetical qualifications and precise numerical details—ten thousand volumes, a forty-minute speech, an increase of 118 subscribers, eight thousand words—lend mock-documentary authority to patently ridiculous circumstances.

Characterization is economical and external. Colonel Telfair is established through his inherited library, antiquated reading, formal appearance, punctilious manners, and fixation on pedigree. Thacker is introduced through comic physical analogy and a hybrid manner supposedly borrowed from several public figures. Neither character receives extensive psychological analysis; instead, personality emerges from clothing, gesture, speech rhythm, cultural references, and responses to manuscripts. The characters verge on types—the unreconstructed Southern antiquarian and the aggressive Northern promoter—but their consistency and verbal distinctiveness keep them vivid.

The story’s structure resembles an extended setup leading to a final reversal. The opening establishes the magazine’s provincial editorial policy and its reverence for genealogy. Thacker’s arrival creates the central conflict and turns the middle of the story into a prolonged comic review of the magazine’s contents. Suspense then gathers around the mysterious eight-thousand-word contribution. Colonel Telfair’s grand description encourages both Thacker and the reader to imagine a profound philosophical work, while his concern about the author’s sectional identity delays the revelation. The ending resolves this tension through a compact visual punch line: Theodore Roosevelt’s message to Congress is accepted only after he is presented as “A Member of the Well-known Bulloch Family, of Georgia.” The typographical imitation of a title page slows the revelation and gives the final name maximum force.

Much of the humour depends on dramatic irony. Colonel Telfair considers himself a rigorous guardian of literary quality, yet his standards are governed by kinship and regional affiliation. Thacker correctly identifies the magazine’s editorial weaknesses, but his own commercial tastes are also satirized through sensational exposés, celebrity features, recycled serial material, and calculated publicity. The story therefore does not simply oppose foolish tradition to enlightened modernity; it sets two forms of cultural absurdity against each other. One worships pedigree and the past, while the other treats literature as saleable content.

The setting is conveyed through emblematic rather than atmospheric detail. Cedar Heights, the inherited library, impoverished land, red gullies, bank-building offices, and Confederate references establish a South caught between aristocratic memory and modern commercial reality. Historical and literary allusions are abundant, but they are usually deployed for comic contrast rather than elevated resonance. Chaucer, Macaulay, Tasso, Thomas Moore, Gettysburg, Bull Run, and Fort Sumter coexist with advertising, circulation figures, breweries, waterworks, and magazine fillers. This collision of high culture, sectional mythology, and mundane business forms the story’s characteristic texture.

Overall, the style is polished, fast-moving, allusive, and epigrammatic. It favours caricature over realism, dialogue over introspection, and cumulative comic detail over elaborate plotting. Its satire remains light in surface manner but exact in design, exposing nepotism, cultural provincialism, antiquarian pride, and commercial vulgarity through verbal contrast and a carefully prepared surprise ending.

## The Latitude of Literature

When the *Southern Zodiac* was incorporated at Chalybeate Junction, Georgia, its prospectus announced that it would preserve the intellectual sovereignty of the South, encourage the flowering of native genius, defend the purity of Anglo-Saxon ideals, and accept advertisements for agricultural implements at twenty cents a line.

The last object was printed in smaller type.

The magazine occupied two rooms above the First State Bank and Fertilizer Company. From its eastern windows could be seen the courthouse, a red cotton warehouse, and the railway track bending northward with an appearance of treachery. From the western windows one looked upon Cedar Heights, the ancestral estate of Colonel Aquila Telfair, editor, scholar, veteran, and custodian of several traditions that had survived chiefly because nobody had lately disturbed them.

The colonel was sixty-four, erect, silver-haired, and dressed in black broadcloth regardless of temperature. He wore a low collar, a black string tie, and a watch chain that crossed his waistcoat with the solemnity of a treaty. His face was narrow and patrician; his beard had retired from the field except for a white imperial under the lower lip. He bowed to ladies, removed his hat before monuments, and never referred to the late sectional disturbance by any name that might imply its conclusion.

At Cedar Heights stood a library of ten thousand volumes inherited from three generations of Telfairs. This sounds impressive until you learn that eight thousand were sermons, agricultural reports, county histories, and incomplete sets of Sir Walter Scott. The colonel had read them all except the agricultural reports. The condition of Cedar Heights demonstrated the omission. Its roof sagged, its cornfields had become red gullies, and its chief crop was family recollection.

Colonel Telfair had been chosen editor of the *Southern Zodiac* because his qualifications were undeniable. His grandfather had entertained Henry Clay for dinner; his father had been wounded at Chickamauga; and the colonel himself, at the age of nine, had carried a dispatch three hundred yards through a rainstorm while wearing a gray cap and suffering from measles. Furthermore, he knew what Tasso had said about glory, what Burke had said about conciliation, and what every Telfair since 1739 had said about every other family in the state.

The directors could hardly have found a more literary man without going outside Georgia, which the charter forbade.

The charter provided that the magazine should publish “the work, thought, aspiration, history, philosophy, poetry, anecdote, moral instruction, agricultural reminiscence, and refined humour of writers born in, descended from, married into, or spiritually sympathetic with the Southern States.”

The phrase “spiritually sympathetic” had been inserted to accommodate a contributor in Ohio whose mother’s second cousin had once owned a turpentine still near Savannah.

The editorial staff was assembled with equal care.

Mrs. Araminta Polk Withers held the department of poetry. Her husband’s uncle had been a brigadier, and her own great-aunt had danced with John C. Calhoun, though whether he knew it was a dance had become uncertain with the passage of time. Mrs. Withers wrote sonnets of nineteen lines, explaining that the South had never submitted to Italian rules of composition.

Professor Lucius Quintard Rusk reviewed books. He had been professor of rhetoric at Ptolemy Female College until that institution was converted into a roller-skating pavilion. Professor Rusk possessed a fine command of semicolons and a letter from Jefferson Davis’s former dentist.

Major Pemberton G. Scroope conducted “Memories of the Field.” He had entered the Confederate service at the age of six weeks when his mother carried him through a camp near Macon. In later years the major described himself as the youngest combatant of the war. A portrait in the office showed him with a cavalry sword in one hand and an infant’s feeding bottle in the other. No enemy had ever disputed the claim.

Miss Sophronia Vane edited “The Confederate Hearthstone.” Her principal credential was an aunt who, according to family testimony, had once been kissed by Stonewall Jackson at a church supper. The aunt had not specified the location of the kiss, and Miss Vane’s dignified silence preserved its military value.

There was also Mr. Absalom Dade, office editor and genealogical examiner, whose task was to inspect manuscripts for errors of ancestry. Mr. Dade could trace any Southern family back to a baron, a bishop, or a man who had signed something. He had only one eye, but with it he detected Northern grandparents at a distance of three generations.

With this organization the *Southern Zodiac* began publication.

Its first number contained an address on “The Influence of Chivalric Institutions upon the Cultivation of Sorghum,” a forty-minute speech delivered at the unveiling of a monument to an unknown picket, twenty-seven pages of blank verse concerning the Battle of Shiloh, and a serial romance entitled *The Lily of Lost Cause Manor*. There were also six poems to mockingbirds, four to magnolias, three to swords, two to graves, and one to a mockingbird singing in a magnolia over a grave upon which lay a sword.

The circulation reached 611.

The second number printed a continuation of the sorghum article, additional verses on Shiloh, and a scholarly inquiry into whether General Lee had taken one lump of sugar or two when visiting the author’s grandmother in 1858. The conclusion was reserved for the next issue.

Circulation advanced to 643, including complimentary copies.

After one year, the directors called a meeting. Even Georgia stockholders occasionally discover that departed glory will not pay a living printer.

Colonel Telfair appeared before them carrying a leather portfolio and the confidence of a man supported by ten thousand unread agricultural reports. He attributed the magazine’s financial condition to “the temporary enfeeblement of public taste under the corrosive pressure of commercial sensationalism.”

The treasurer attributed it to $4,800 in unpaid printing bills.

The colonel pointed out that the *Zodiac* had won honourable mention from the Ladies’ Historical Circle of Little Mulberry County. The treasurer replied that the printer did not accept honourable mention at the bank.

It was then that Providence, which sometimes travels under a derby hat, sent Mr. T. T. Thacker from New York.

Thacker promoted magazines. He had promoted a monthly devoted to vegetarian athletics, a weekly for amateur detectives, and a trade journal called *The Undertaker’s Smile*. He had raised the circulation of the last by offering a free accident-insurance policy with every annual subscription.

Physically he resembled a well-fed terrier that had acquired banking connections. He was short, alert, glossy, and equipped with eyes that counted everything in the room, including the buttons on your coat. His speech combined the speed of a telegraph instrument, the cordiality of a campaign manager, and the conscience of a slot machine.

He arrived in Chalybeate Junction with two suitcases, a portable typewriter, and a plan.

“I’ve looked you over,” he told the directors, “and you’ve got the finest undeveloped cemetery in American journalism. The name is good, the territory is good, and the magazine is deader than Julius Caesar’s campaign committee. That means opportunity.”

The directors did not wholly approve of his imagery, but they approved of his offer. Thacker would invest ten thousand dollars, take charge of promotion, and increase the circulation to fifty thousand within a year. In return he demanded a voice in editorial policy.

Colonel Telfair rose.

“Gentlemen,” he said, “while I should be reluctant to interpose objections to an arrangement calculated to relieve the present pecuniary embarrassment of this institution, I must nevertheless insist that no alien hand be permitted to impair its essential character. The *Southern Zodiac* was founded not as a receptacle for the ephemeral productions of every scribbling adventurer who may obtain notoriety in Boston, Chicago, or other centres of intellectual unrest, but as a sanctuary wherein the genius of our own people might find dignified and uncontaminated expression.”

“Sure,” said Thacker. “Keep the sanctuary. I only want to put a cash register in the vestibule.”

Thus they became associates.

On his first morning in the office Thacker removed his coat, pushed back his cuffs, and examined three months’ manuscripts. He worked for two hours in silence while Colonel Telfair wrote an editorial entitled “The Assault of Modernity upon the Rural Verities.”

At eleven, Thacker lit a cigar.

“Colonel,” he said, “where do you get this truck?”

The colonel slowly raised his head.

“If by ‘truck,’ Mr. Thacker, you intend a general designation of the literary material at present before you, I may say that it represents the spontaneous efflorescence of Southern culture.”

“It represents spontaneous combustion,” said Thacker. “If we print it, the subscribers will burn the office.”

He held up a manuscript.

“Here’s fourteen thousand words on ‘Recollections of My Father’s Stable Boy’s Grandmother.’ What’s it got?”

“The author is a Fitzhugh of Virginia.”

“Does that make the stable boy’s grandmother move any faster?”

“The Fitzhughs,” said the colonel, “require no acceleration.”

Thacker picked up another contribution.

“‘Lines Written on Seeing the Bust of a Statesman in the Hallway of a Macon Hotel.’ Nine pages. Who did this?”

“A direct descendant of the Rutledges.”

“And this—‘Was Pocahontas Misunderstood?’”

“The writer’s maternal grandfather commanded a battery at Vicksburg.”

“What did Pocahontas command?”

Colonel Telfair looked pained.

“Your jibes, sir, while perhaps consonant with the lighter standards of metropolitan intercourse, do not facilitate an equitable consideration of the matter.”

“All right. No jibes. Let’s consider it as a business. I’ve got a magazine with twelve hundred subscribers, seven hundred of whom are cousins of the contributors. The other five hundred think they subscribed to the *Southern Poultry Guide*. We need names. We need stories with people in them that do something before page six. We need pictures, gossip, mystery, love, crime, money, and one article every month that makes the reader afraid his neighbour knows more than he does.”

“The function of literature,” said Colonel Telfair, “is to elevate.”

“Certainly. But first you’ve got to get it off the floor.”

Thacker began walking about the room.

“I can get Gilroy Haines to do us a Washington article. I can buy a sea story from Captain Bludsoe—the man’s been wrecked in every ocean except the Arctic, and he’s leaving Thursday. We’ll run ‘How Our Millionaires Choose Their Wives,’ with photographs. We’ll get an actress to tell why she never married; that always interests her three husbands. Then a detective serial, a page of jokes, and something about food that poisons you slowly. Put a red cover on it. Bang! Thirty thousand by Christmas.”

Colonel Telfair’s lips contracted.

“And these persons whom you propose to introduce into our pages—may I inquire whether any possess affiliations with the South?”

“They possess affiliations with the public.”

“That is not synonymous.”

“It is at the news stand.”

The colonel laid down his pen.

“Mr. Thacker, I do not deny that the expansion of our circulation is desirable. I do not deny that contemporary themes may, under restrictions, merit consideration. But I cannot consent to fling open these portals to every Northern manufacturer of literary merchandise merely because his name has acquired currency among readers of unstable taste.”

“Then don’t fling. Open ’em six inches and charge admission.”

“Our contributors have hitherto been selected with regard to character, culture, tradition, and the possession of a viewpoint harmonious with that of the magazine.”

“You left out kinfolk.”

“I did not consider it necessary to state the obvious.”

Thacker laughed.

“Colonel, you’re a wonder. You don’t edit a magazine; you hold a family reunion in type.”

For a week the two men fenced across the editorial table.

Thacker submitted an article by a Chicago surgeon on appendicitis. Colonel Telfair rejected it because the surgeon had served as medical adviser to a Grand Army post. The colonel offered instead “Plantation Remedies Recalled by an Octogenarian,” which recommended sassafras tea for fractures.

Thacker proposed a story by the most popular woman novelist in the country. Colonel Telfair’s investigation showed that she had been born in Massachusetts. He suggested a substitution by Mrs. Araminta Polk Withers, whose romance concerned two lovers separated for ninety years by a misunderstanding at a barbecue.

Thacker wanted an exposé of municipal corruption.

The colonel offered a twelve-page account of a banquet given to Alexander H. Stephens.

Thacker demanded humour.

Colonel Telfair supplied “Droll Sayings of Faithful Retainers,” in which an elderly servant said, “Yes, Marse William,” on five different occasions.

The promoter grew desperate.

“You can’t sell embalmed recollections forever,” he said. “The country wants now. It wants electricity, automobiles, trusts, divorces, airships, politics, prize fights. It wants a man who was in the White House yesterday telling what somebody whispered behind a curtain. It doesn’t want Cousin Clementina remembering what Uncle Beauregard almost said in 1860.”

“Cousin Clementina,” said the colonel, “is a woman of irreproachable veracity.”

“That’s her trouble. She never improves anything.”

Yet Thacker did accomplish changes. He doubled the advertising pages, introduced illustrations, reduced Major Scroope’s reminiscences from thirty pages to eight, and persuaded the colonel to print a short story by a Kentucky writer whose grandfather had moved from New Jersey before the war. Mr. Dade examined the genealogy for three days and pronounced the taint technically extinguished by climate.

Circulation increased by 118.

Thacker celebrated as if he had annexed Canada.

Then, one rainy afternoon, he entered the colonel’s office and found the editor reading a thick typewritten manuscript. Colonel Telfair was so absorbed that he failed to hear the promoter knock, enter, cough, move a chair, and drop a bound volume of *Debates in the Provisional Congress*.

Thacker’s eyes brightened.

“Good stuff?”

Colonel Telfair placed one long hand upon the manuscript.

“It is a contribution of exceptional interest.”

“Story?”

“No.”

“Scandal?”

“Certainly not.”

“Politics?”

“In the broadest and most elevated interpretation of that term.”

“Who wrote it?”

The colonel hesitated.

“The identity of the author need not at present concern us.”

Thacker sat down.

“When an editor says that, the author’s either famous or in jail. How long?”

“Approximately eight thousand words.”

“Eight thousand!” Thacker leaned forward. “And you like it?”

“I find in it breadth, vigour, lucidity, moral earnestness, a robust comprehension of national responsibilities, and a directness of utterance not wholly devoid of literary merit.”

“Then buy it.”

“The question is not so simple.”

“It’s always simple when the copy’s good. Who’s the man?”

Colonel Telfair adjusted his string tie.

“He is widely known.”

“North or South?”

The colonel’s silence answered.

Thacker slapped his knee.

“Well, sound the trumpets! A Northerner has crossed the Rappahannock and reached your desk alive.”

“I have not stated that the manuscript will be accepted.”

“But you want it.”

“I recognize its power.”

“Then run it.”

“Before taking a step of such gravity, I must satisfy myself that the author is not entirely alien to the traditions represented by this publication.”

Thacker stared at him.

“You mean you’re going to look up his grandmother?”

“I propose to institute a discreet genealogical inquiry.”

“Colonel, if Shakespeare mailed you *Hamlet*, you’d hold it until you found out whether the Prince of Denmark had an uncle in Mobile.”

“The geographical affiliations of Shakespeare,” said Colonel Telfair, “present questions of considerable complexity.”

Thacker got up and paced.

“Who is it? Senator? Ambassador? College president? Railroad king?”

“I am not at liberty to say.”

“Does he live in New York?”

“That inquiry is irrelevant.”

“Boston?”

“Mr. Thacker—”

“Washington?”

The colonel folded the manuscript and placed it in a drawer.

“I must ask you to respect the confidentiality customarily accorded to material under editorial consideration.”

Thacker bent over the desk.

“I’ll bet you fifty dollars you print it.”

“I do not wager upon matters involving principle.”

“Twenty-five.”

“No.”

“A dinner.”

“I decline.”

“A barrel of your favourite mineral water.”

Colonel Telfair’s expression softened almost imperceptibly. The Chalybeate Junction mineral water tasted like a horseshoe dissolved in rain, but he regarded it as medicinal.

“I cannot participate in a bet,” he said. “Nevertheless, should the contribution prove admissible, I would have no objection to your commemorating the event in whatever harmless fashion may recommend itself.”

“That’s a bet with a funeral veil over it,” said Thacker. “Done.”

During the next two weeks Colonel Telfair conducted his investigation.

He wrote letters to Charleston, Savannah, Roswell, and Oyster Bay. He consulted county histories, family Bibles, obituaries, army records, marriage announcements, and a volume entitled *Distinguished Georgians and Those Who Ought to Have Been*. He interviewed Mrs. Withers, Professor Rusk, and an elderly judge who could remember every family connection in the state except his own first wife.

Mr. Dade was called in and supplied with maps.

The genealogical examiner worked with impressive solemnity. He filled sheets of foolscap with branching lines that resembled river systems afflicted by drought. Names were circled, connected, questioned, underlined, and pursued through marriages. A Bulloch joined a Stewart; a Stewart encountered an Elliott; an Elliott wandered toward a Roosevelt; then the trail divided, crossed Long Island, returned by way of Philadelphia, and disappeared behind a second cousin’s baptism.

Thacker watched these operations from the adjoining room.

“Any Confederate cavalry in the underbrush?” he asked.

Mr. Dade gave no answer.

“Find a Georgia uncle yet?”

Silence.

“How about a cook who once heard of Atlanta?”

Mr. Dade closed the door.

The mystery began to trouble Thacker. He knew every prominent writer then selling words by the pound, yard, or reputation. He telegraphed two literary agents in New York and wrote to a correspondent in Washington. He inspected the colonel’s wastebasket, but discovered only a rejected ode to a courthouse bell and a note ordering shoe polish.

One evening he met Colonel Telfair at the railway station.

The colonel held a telegram and appeared almost cheerful.

“Good news from the family cemetery?” Thacker asked.

“I have received information of a confirmatory nature.”

“So our Northern genius has a rebel rib somewhere in his skeleton?”

“I should not employ that metaphor, but substantial evidence of an ancestral connection with this state has been established.”

“Close connection?”

“Blood, sir, admits no measurement in terms of mileage.”

“Grandfather?”

“I prefer not to anticipate publication.”

“Great-grandmother?”

The colonel bowed and entered his carriage.

Thacker stood under the station lamp and watched him drive away toward Cedar Heights. The promoter’s face wore the expression of a man who has heard a safe click but cannot find the door.

On the following Monday the *Southern Zodiac* went to press.

Thacker was in Atlanta arranging a contract with a lithographer for a new cover—a spirited female figure representing the South, holding a laurel wreath in one hand and a subscription blank in the other. He returned late Thursday evening. The town was dark except for the bank clock and the windows of the printing office.

He climbed the stairs and found Colonel Telfair correcting proofs.

“Well?” said Thacker.

“The issue has been completed.”

“Did the eight-thousand-word blockbuster get in?”

“It did.”

Thacker whistled.

“Name?”

“You will receive a copy in the morning.”

“Colonel, I’ve waited two weeks.”

“A few additional hours can impose no serious hardship.”

“Did you prove he belonged to Georgia?”

“I established that his lineage includes one of the most respected families in the state.”

“Then I owe you mineral water.”

Colonel Telfair inclined his head.

“The water may be sent to Cedar Heights.”

At nine the next morning a printer’s boy delivered the first bound copy of the new issue to Thacker’s hotel. He tore off the wrapper before the boy reached the stairs.

The cover had been altered. Instead of Thacker’s spirited female figure, it bore an engraving of a columned mansion under a live oak. Beneath appeared the legend:

**THE SOUTHERN ZODIAC**  
*A Monthly Exponent of Native Letters, History, and Ideals*

Thacker turned the pages.

There was Mrs. Withers’s poem, “To a Sabre Found in an Attic.” There was Professor Rusk’s review of a biography published eleven years before. There was Major Scroope, describing how he had personally witnessed the retreat from Atlanta from a cradle in a nearby county. There was “The Lily of Lost Cause Manor,” now in its fourteenth chapter and still on the veranda.

Then Thacker came upon eight pages of heavy type.

At the top stood an ornamental heading surrounded by magnolia blossoms, crossed flags, and a small outline of the state of Georgia. Below it, in dignified capitals, was printed:

### A MESSAGE UPON THE AFFAIRS  
### AND DUTIES OF THE NATION

#### By a Distinguished American Statesman

Thacker read the first paragraph. His mouth opened.

He turned back to the title page. Beneath the heading, in smaller type, the colonel had inserted an editorial note:

> The *Southern Zodiac* takes especial pride in presenting to its readers this vigorous and important state paper from the pen of an American whose maternal ancestry identifies him intimately with Georgia. Through his mother, Martha Bulloch, he derives from the historic Bulloch family, long honoured in the annals of this commonwealth. In welcoming this contribution, therefore, we do not depart from our established policy, but rather extend recognition to a distinguished representative of Southern blood.

Then came the author’s name:

### THEODORE ROOSEVELT  
### PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES  
### AND A MEMBER OF THE WELL-KNOWN  
### BULLOCH FAMILY OF GEORGIA

Thacker read it twice. He sat down on the bed. Presently he began to laugh, and the brass pitcher rattled on the washstand.

At ten o’clock he entered the editorial office carrying the magazine under one arm and an order for a barrel of Chalybeate water under the other.

Colonel Telfair was opening his mail.

“Colonel,” said Thacker, “you win. You’ve captured the President.”

“I have merely presented the facts of his maternal descent.”

“You’ve annexed him to Georgia.”

“Blood relationship,” replied the colonel, “is not annexation.”

Thacker laid the order on the desk.

“There’s your mineral water. Thirty gallons. If it doesn’t kill you, nothing can.”

The colonel examined the paper and bowed.

“Your courtesy is appreciated.”

Thacker turned to go, then stopped.

“One thing more. If the King of England sends us an article, can we print it?”

Colonel Telfair considered.

“The question would require investigation.”

“I suppose so. Maybe his third nurse had a cousin in Augusta.”

“Mr. Thacker,” said the colonel with dignity, “your levity continually leads you into historical inaccuracy.”

That month the *Southern Zodiac* gained 7,400 subscribers. Thacker advertised the President’s message in every newspaper from New York to New Orleans, omitting only the genealogy. Colonel Telfair regarded the increase as a triumph of Southern letters.

And perhaps it was. For the South had supplied the author, the North had supplied the circulation, Congress had supplied the copy, and the President of the United States had contributed without being asked.

This is known in magazine offices as editorial cooperation.

### The Lighthouse Keeper’s Library

Every morning, before the gulls began their quarrels, Elias Vale climbed the spiral stairs of the lighthouse and extinguished the lamp.

He had performed the task for thirty-one years. His knees had learned the number of steps better than his mind had: one hundred and forty-two from the kitchen to the lantern room, with the last seven narrowed by the curve of the wall. In darkness, in fog, even half asleep, Elias never stumbled.

The lighthouse stood on Grayhaven Island, a long strip of black rock three miles from the mainland. Nothing grew there except coarse grass, thorn bushes, and a single bent pine that leaned permanently toward the east, as though trying to escape.

Elias lived alone.

Once a month, a supply boat came from the harbor with lamp oil, flour, coffee, and letters. The boatman, Tom Bell, was a cheerful young man who regarded silence as an illness requiring immediate treatment.

“You’ll turn into a barnacle out here,” Tom often said.

“Barnacles don’t pay taxes,” Elias replied.

“Nor do they read newspapers from six months ago.”

“The news improves with age. By the time it reaches me, most of it has stopped mattering.”

Tom never understood whether Elias was joking.

In addition to supplies, the boat carried books. Grayhaven Lighthouse possessed a small library, though it had never officially been given one. The collection had begun when Elias’s wife, Miriam, moved to the island with six crates of novels. Over the years, visitors and sailors had added their own volumes: adventure stories swollen by damp, romances without covers, dictionaries missing entire sections of the alphabet, and histories written with more confidence than truth.

Miriam had arranged them on shelves throughout the lighthouse. Books lined the kitchen walls, occupied the cupboard beneath the stairs, and climbed in uneven towers beside the bed.

“Stories keep a house warm,” she used to say.

After she died, Elias did not move a single book.

That was twelve years ago.

On the morning the first blue book arrived, the sea was calm enough to resemble hammered metal. Tom tied his boat to the small stone pier and hauled up the usual sacks.

“Package for you,” he said.

“I didn’t order anything.”

“That’s what makes it exciting.”

The parcel was wrapped in brown paper and tied with white string. No address appeared on it except Elias’s name, written in narrow black letters.

Inside was a book bound in blue cloth. It had no title, no author’s name, and no publisher’s mark. Its pages were blank.

“A very peaceful read,” Tom said, looking over Elias’s shoulder.

Elias turned the book upside down and shook it. Nothing fell out.

“Maybe it’s a journal.”

“I have nothing to write.”

“Everyone has something to write.”

“Then everyone else can do it.”

Tom laughed, drank two cups of Elias’s coffee, and left before the tide turned.

Elias placed the blue book on a table in the kitchen. All day it irritated him. Among the stained and battered books Miriam had collected, its clean cover seemed almost rude. That evening, he carried it upstairs, intending to bury it on an empty shelf.

As he did, the book opened in his hands.

Words covered the first page.

Elias stared. He was certain the pages had been blank.

The handwriting was black and precise.

At seven minutes past midnight, the eastern lantern pane will crack.

He read the sentence twice. Then he examined the remaining pages, but they were empty.

The wind was light that night. No storm approached. The glass panes surrounding the lamp were thick, polished, and inspected each morning. Elias checked the eastern pane and found no flaw.

At midnight, he remained in the lantern room with his arms folded.

Seven minutes later, a gull struck the glass.

The sound was like a pistol shot. The bird vanished into darkness, leaving a smear of feathers and blood. Across the eastern pane ran a thin white crack.

Elias stood without moving.

Then he descended the stairs, opened the blue book, and found a second sentence beneath the first.

Tomorrow, the supply boat will not come.

“Of course it won’t,” Elias muttered. “It came today.”

When he looked again, the word tomorrow had changed.

Next month, the supply boat will not come.

For the next four weeks, Elias tried to forget the book. He replaced the cracked pane and returned to his routine. He cleaned the lens, trimmed the wick, recorded the weather, and read old novels in which lost fortunes were recovered and lovers endured exactly as much misery as necessary.

Yet every night he opened the blue book.

No new words appeared.

On the first Monday of the following month, Elias watched the horizon from dawn until evening. Tom’s boat did not come.

Nor did it come the next day.

On Wednesday, the sky darkened. By afternoon, the sea had grown violent, and waves broke across the pier.

Shortly after sunset, Elias saw a flash between the swells.

He climbed to the lantern room and lifted the telescope. A small boat drifted south of the island, its sail torn. Someone aboard was signaling with a mirror.

Elias lit a hand lantern, pulled on his coat, and made his way down the cliff path. No proper rescue boat was kept on Grayhaven; the old rowboat by the pier was little more than a floating bucket. Nevertheless, he dragged it into the surf.

The sea threw him back twice. On his third attempt, he passed the rocks and began rowing.

He found Tom clinging to the overturned hull of the supply boat.

“You’re late,” Elias shouted.

Tom attempted a laugh but swallowed seawater instead.

Getting him into the rowboat nearly capsized them both. By the time they reached shore, Elias’s hands were bleeding and Tom had lost consciousness.

For two days, fever burned through the young man. Elias gave him Miriam’s old room and sat beside the bed through the nights. On the third morning, Tom woke and asked for coffee.

“You’re in no condition for coffee,” Elias said.

“Then tea.”

“You dislike tea.”

“I’ve been near death. It broadened my tastes.”

Elias made coffee.

Tom remained on the island for nine days while his strength returned. He spoke less than usual. His boat had struck a submerged object during the storm, though he insisted no rocks should have been in that part of the channel.

“Something hit from underneath,” he said. “Something hard.”

“Driftwood.”

“Driftwood doesn’t ring like a bell.”

On the seventh evening, Elias found Tom in the kitchen with the blue book open before him.

“Where did you get this?” Tom asked.

“It came on your boat.”

“I mean the writing.”

Elias stopped.

A third sentence had appeared.

When the bell rings beneath the sea, the dead ship will enter the harbor.

Tom read it aloud, then looked up.

Elias closed the book. “It enjoys being mysterious.”

“You knew my boat wouldn’t come.”

“I knew what the book claimed.”

“And you never thought to warn me?”

“How? You brought the warning yourself, and by the time I read it, you were gone.”

Tom glanced at the ceiling, as if imagining the dark floors above them and the tower beyond.

“My grandmother told me stories about a bell under Grayhaven.”

“Grandmothers are responsible for a large percentage of the world’s nonsense.”

“She said a passenger ship sank near here before the lighthouse was built. The Saint Orison.”

Elias knew the name. Everyone along the coast did. The Saint Orison had vanished ninety years earlier with more than two hundred people aboard. No wreckage was ever found.

“When storms come from the north,” Tom continued, “fishermen say they hear its bell. Then they see lights moving under the water.”

“You heard metal when your boat struck something, and now your imagination is filling the gaps.”

“What is that book filling?”

Elias had no answer.

When Tom finally returned to the mainland in a borrowed fishing boat, he took the blue book with him. Elias allowed it. He was relieved to see it go.

For three months, life at Grayhaven returned to normal.

Then the letters began.

Tom wrote that he had shown the book to a schoolteacher, a priest, the harbor master, and finally an elderly woman named Alice Wren. Mrs. Wren’s grandfather had been a child aboard the Saint Orison. According to family history, he had survived because a sailor placed him in a storage chest before the ship went down. The chest washed ashore two days later.

In his fourth letter, Tom wrote:

Mrs. Wren says the book belonged to the ship’s librarian. They called him Mr. Blue because he always wore a blue coat. Passengers visited him to have their fortunes written. Every prediction came true, but never in the way they expected. On the night the ship vanished, he wrote only one line: The lighthouse will fail when the dead come home.

Elias read the sentence several times.

There had been no lighthouse when the Saint Orison sank.

Tom’s next letter contained worse news. Words were appearing rapidly in the blue book. Some were harmless predictions. A dog would steal a red scarf. The mayor would fall asleep during a speech. A church window would break in clear weather.

All had occurred.

Then the book had written about Grayhaven.

On the longest night, the keeper will choose between the light and the living.

The longest night of the year was three weeks away.

Elias replied at once.

Burn the book.

Tom’s answer came by the next supply boat.

We tried.

That was all.

Winter pressed down upon the island. Frost whitened the rocks, and the sea became the color of iron. Elias worked longer hours in the lantern room, checking every gear and polishing the great lens until it scattered rainbows across the walls.

The lighthouse must not fail.

The phrase followed him through his days.

He told himself it was duty, nothing more. Ships depended on the Grayhaven light. Without it, the reef north of the island was invisible at night. Yet beneath that practical concern lay another fear, quieter and more difficult to admit.

Miriam had died because the light had failed once before.

It had happened during a storm. A gear in the rotation mechanism snapped shortly before midnight. Elias climbed outside to reach the maintenance platform, leaving Miriam below with instructions to keep the emergency lamp burning.

While he repaired the mechanism, she saw distress lights near the western rocks.

She took the rowboat.

Elias never saw her alive again.

Her boat was found two days later, empty and undamaged. No distressed vessel was ever reported. No body came ashore.

For twelve years, Elias had replayed that night. If he had remained below, he might have stopped her. If he had repaired the gear sooner, she might not have mistaken the distant lights for a ship. If he had gone after her—

But regret was a wheel that turned without moving.

On the afternoon of December twenty-first, Tom arrived with the blue book sealed inside a metal box.

“You shouldn’t have come,” Elias said.

“Good to see you too.”

Tom unloaded fuel, blankets, and enough food for a week. The sky was already darkening.

“I’m staying tonight,” he said.

“No.”

“That wasn’t a request.”

Elias looked at the northern horizon. Clouds formed a black wall above the water.

“Then make yourself useful.”

They secured the shutters, checked the emergency lamps, and carried extra oil to the lantern room. As darkness fell, the storm reached them.

Wind struck the lighthouse with a deep, continuous roar. Waves exploded against the island, sending spray over the kitchen windows. In the lantern room, the great light revolved steadily, its beam sweeping across rain and darkness.

At eleven, the bell began.

It came from beneath the sea.

Each slow note trembled up through the tower stones. The sound was too vast to belong to any ordinary ship, and too deep to be mistaken for thunder.

Tom gripped the railing. “You hear it.”

“Yes.”

They saw the Saint Orison at half past eleven.

It emerged from the northern storm, a black ship with three tall funnels and rows of golden windows. Water poured from its decks. Torn ropes moved like weeds along its sides. Figures crowded the railings, pale faces turned toward the lighthouse.

The ship was heading directly for the reef.

Elias seized the signal lever and sounded the foghorn.

The Saint Orison did not change course.

Tom opened the metal box. Inside, the blue book’s pages turned by themselves, though there was no wind in the room. Writing spilled across them.

The keeper will choose between the light and the living.

Below those words, another line appeared.

The lost woman waits where the beam does not reach.

Elias looked west.

Beyond the sweep of the lantern, a small light shone near the rocks.

Three flashes. A pause. Three more.

Miriam had used that signal whenever she returned late from the mainland.

“No,” Elias whispered.

He took the telescope. The beam passed over the western sea, and for an instant he saw a rowboat rising on a wave.

A woman sat inside it.

Her red coat was faded, her dark hair streaked with gray. She raised one hand.

Elias dropped the telescope.

Tom had seen her too. His face had gone white.

The Saint Orison’s bell sounded again. The floor shuddered. Cracks appeared in the lantern panes.

“Miriam,” Elias said.

The rowboat was drifting toward the western rocks. He had only minutes to reach her.

At the same time, the dead ship advanced toward the reef. If the lighthouse beam continued its rotation, it would guide the Saint Orison into Grayhaven Harbor, where dozens of boats and waterfront houses lay in its path. If Elias extinguished the lamp, the ship might turn away—or it might strike the reef and break apart.

And if he left the tower, the damaged lantern could fail on its own.

The choice between the light and the living.

Elias stared at the blue book.

Then he began to laugh.

It was not joyful laughter. It was hard and breathless and close to anger.

Tom stepped back. “What is it?”

“The book is a liar.”

“It’s never been wrong.”

“That isn’t the same thing.”

Elias picked up the book. “It tells just enough truth to make cowards of us. It offers two doors and hopes we won’t notice the wall is rotten.”

He carried it to the central lamp.

The pages fluttered wildly.

Elias tore them out by the handful and fed them into the flame.

The paper burned blue.

New words appeared even as the pages blackened.

THE LIGHT WILL FAIL.

Elias continued.

THE SHIP WILL ENTER THE HARBOR.

He thrust the final page into the fire.

THE WOMAN WILL BE LOST.

The book collapsed into ash.

For one second, nothing happened.

Then every pane in the lantern room shattered.

Wind burst through the chamber. The flame stretched sideways and vanished. Darkness swallowed the lighthouse.

Outside, the Saint Orison sounded its bell.

“Emergency lamp!” Elias shouted.

He and Tom descended. Halfway down, the tower lurched. Books fell from shelves, striking the stairs around them. In the kitchen, Elias grabbed two hand lanterns and a coil of rope.

“To the western shore,” he said.

“What about the lighthouse?”

“We are the lighthouse.”

They ran into the storm.

At the cliff edge, Elias tied one end of the rope around his waist and gave the other to Tom. The rowboat appeared below, trapped between waves and rock.

Miriam looked up at him.

She had not aged a day.

Elias climbed down.

The rocks were slick with ice and seaweed. Twice he lost his footing, and twice Tom held the rope. When he reached the lowest ledge, the rowboat surged toward him.

Miriam stretched out her hand.

Their fingers touched.

She was warm.

“Elias,” she said, as if they had parted that morning.

A shadow rose behind her.

The Saint Orison towered above the island, impossibly close. Its decks were crowded with the dead. Their mouths opened together, and from them came the tolling of the bell.

Elias pulled Miriam from the boat.

“Now!” he shouted.

Tom hauled the rope. A wave struck them, crushing Elias against the cliff. He refused to release her. Inch by inch, they climbed until Tom seized Miriam’s wrist and dragged them both over the edge.

The dead ship turned toward the harbor.

Its golden windows passed like a city through the rain.

Elias lit his hand lantern.

“Tom, take Miriam to the eastern point. Hold the lantern low and steady.”

“What are you going to do?”

“Give the ship a choice.”

There were six emergency lamps in the lighthouse. Together they carried them outside and placed them along the northern cliff. Elias arranged five in a curving line toward the reef. He kept the sixth dark.

From the sea, the lamps resembled harbor lights marking a safe channel.

The Saint Orison turned toward them.

“Now run,” Elias said.

They retreated as the ship approached the false harbor. Its bow passed through the outer rocks as if through mist, but when its hull reached the reef, the island shook.

A great crack split the night.

For a moment, the Saint Orison stood still. Then the sea rose through it.

The dead passengers lifted their faces. Elias expected cries, but instead he heard sighs—hundreds of sighs, like sleepers releasing a final breath.

The golden windows went dark.

The ship dissolved into rain.

Silence fell over Grayhaven.

At dawn, the storm ended.

Elias, Tom, and Miriam sat in the kitchen beneath blankets. No one had spoken for nearly an hour.

Miriam held a cup of coffee between both hands. She had told them what little she remembered. On the night she vanished, she had followed lights to the western rocks. She heard a bell. Then came darkness.

To her, only a few minutes had passed.

Elias looked older than she did now. She touched the gray in his beard with quiet wonder.

“I’m sorry,” she said.

“For what?”

“Leaving.”

He covered her hand with his. “You came back.”

Outside, morning sunlight lay across a sea filled with floating pages. Some were ancient and stained; others were white and blank. They drifted around the island like a flock of resting birds.

The lighthouse itself was badly damaged. Every lantern pane had shattered, and the lens had cracked from top to bottom.

Elias climbed the one hundred and forty-two steps to see it.

Miriam came with him.

At the top, wind moved freely through the ruined chamber. The horizon was clear. Far away, rescue boats were already approaching from the mainland, following Tom’s emergency signal.

“What will you do?” Miriam asked.

Elias looked at the broken lamp.

For thirty-one years, he had believed his duty was to keep one light burning in one tower. Now the old certainty seemed too small.

“Rebuild,” he said.

“The lighthouse?”

He smiled.

They converted Grayhaven Lighthouse into a rescue station the following spring. Tom became its first captain. Miriam reopened the library and placed a wooden box beside the door with a sign asking visitors to leave a story and take another.

Elias remained keeper, though the title no longer meant what it once had.

Ships still relied on Grayhaven’s beam. Sailors still reported strange lights during northern storms, but the bell beneath the sea was never heard again.

As for the blue book, only one fragment survived. Miriam found it caught beneath a stone on the western shore. It was badly burned, and most of its words had vanished.

She kept the fragment framed above the library desk.

Visitors often asked what it said.

The sentence was incomplete.

The keeper will choose—

Nothing followed.

The rest of the page remained blank.
